name: February 2, 2022 Regular Meeting
agenda_text:
This meeting will be held via teleconference only in order to reduce the risk of spreading COVID-
19 and pursuant to AB 361 and the County of Los Angeles Public Health Officer’s Order (revised
January 10, 2022). All votes taken during this teleconference meeting will be by roll call vote, and
the vote will be publicly reported.

HOW TO VIEW THE MEETING: No physical location from which members of the public may
observe the meeting and offer public comment will be provided. Please view the meeting, which will be
live streamed at https://malibucity.org/video and https://malibucity.org/VirtualMeeting.

HOW TO PARTICIPATE BEFORE THE MEETING: Members of the public are encouraged to
submit email correspondence to mlinden@malibucity.org before the meeting begins.

HOW TO PARTICIPATE DURING THE MEETING: Members of the public may speak during the
meeting through the Zoom application. You must first sign up to speak before the item you would like
to speak on has been called by the Chair and then you must be present in the Zoom conference to be
recognized.

Please visit https://malibucity.org/VirtualMeeting and follow the directions for signing up to speak and
downloading the Zoom application.

  Guide to the City Commission Proceedings

As a result of the Coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, the City is under a state of local emergency, as well as states of
emergency that have been declared in the County of Los Angeles, State of California, and a federal emergency
declared by the President of the United States. In order to reduce the risk of spreading COVID-19, the Commission
meeting will be open and public but conducted virtually because meeting in person would present imminent risks to
the health or safety of attendees. This way, the public, the staff, and the Commission will not be physically in the same
place.
The Oral Communication portion of the agenda is for members of the public to present items which are not listed on the
agenda but are under the subject matter jurisdiction of the Commission. Although no action may be taken, the Commission
and staff will follow up, at an appropriate time, on those items needing response. Each speaker is limited to three (3) minutes.
Members of the public wishing to speak during the meeting must participate through the Zoom application. You must first
sign up to speak before the item you would like to speak on has been called by the Chair and then you must be present in the
Zoom conference to be recognized. Please visit https://MalibuCity.org/VirtualMeeting and follow the directions for signing
up to speak and downloading the Zoom application.
Items in Consent Calendar Section A have already been considered by the Commission at a previous meeting where the
public was invited to comment, after which a decision was made. These items are not subject to public discussion at this
meeting because the vote taken at the previous meeting was final. Resolutions concerning decisions made at previous
meetings are for the purpose of memorializing the decision to assure the accuracy of the findings, the prior vote, and any
conditions imposed.
Items in Consent Calendar Section B have not been discussed previously by the Commission. If discussion is desired, an
item may be removed from the Consent Calendar for individual consideration. Commissioners may indicate a negative or
abstaining vote on any individual item by so declaring prior to the vote on the motion to adopt the entire Consent
Calendar. Items excluded from the Consent Calendar will be taken up by the Commission following the action on the Consent
Calendar. The Commission first will take up the items for which public speaker requests have been submitted. Public speakers
shall follow the rules as set forth under Oral Communication.
Old Business items have appeared on previous agendas but have either been continued or tabled to this meeting with no final
action having been taken. Public comment shall follow the rules as set forth under Oral Communication.
Items in New Business are items which are appearing for the first time for formal action. Public comment shall follow the
rules as set forth under Oral Communication.
Copies of the staff reports or other written documentation relating to each item of business described above are on file in the
office of the City Manager, and available upon request by emailing MLinden@MalibuCity.org.
The City Hall phone number is (310) 456-2489. To contact City Hall using a telecommunication device for the deaf (TDD),
please call (800) 735-2929 and a California Relay Service operator will assist you. In compliance with the Americans with
Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this meeting, please contact Yolanda Bundy, Environmental
Sustainability Director, at (310) 456-2489, ext. 229. Notification 48 hours prior to the meeting will enable the City to make
reasonable arrangements to ensure accessibility to this meeting. [28 CFR 35.102-35.104 ADD Title II].
I hereby certify under penalty of perjury, under the laws of the State of California, that the foregoing agenda was posted in
accordance with the applicable legal requirements. Dated this 26th day of January 2022, at 11:00 a.m.

ITEM 1.B.  STAFF UPDATES

  Public Works Superintendent Aladjadjian provided an update on the City’s
  response to last week’s storm event. He stated all roads were now open.

  Vice Chair Stewart requested advice for homeowners on private roads during storm
  events. Public Works Superintendent Aladjadjian confirmed City workers would
  not go on private roads. He stated homeowner associations often had contractors
  on call. He stated the Fire Department could assist with downed trees.

  Public Safety Manager Dueñas stated the Governor declared a state of emergency
  for the storms allowing for potential reimbursement of costs for the City’s response.
  She stated the City assisted American Red Cross with setting up a shelter at Malibu
  High School for Leo Carrillo State Beach evacuees. She announced City Hall was
  closed to the public for the rest of January due to a rise in COVID-19 cases. She
  stated staff were still available to provide services. She reminded Commissioners
  they could assist with the Homeless Count on January 26 at 6:30 a.m.

  Public Safety Liaison Flores confirmed the City was working closely with the
  County to get the word out about the Homeless Count.

  Fire Safety Liaison Brossard stated 2021 was a good year for Malibu with only
  about five acres burned within the city limits. He stated fuel moisture levels were
  currently at 79 percent. He stated hazard tree removal continued with 18 properties
  visited, and 38 trees removed, using approximately $88,000 of the $300,000
  budget. He stated the removals would resume next week.

ITEM 1.C.  COMMISSIONER COMMENTS

  Ex Officio Member Woodworth agreed with Fire Safety Liaison Brossard that
  Malibu was lucky in 2021. He commended the Fire Department for being proactive.
  He recommended the City and Fire Department continue efforts to get homeowners
  to address fire risks on their property. He discussed non-profit organizations
  working on fire mitigation. He suggested the City push utilities to provide better
  information about power shutoffs and keeping communication lines open during
  power outages. He suggested businesses along PCH remain open during
  evacuations. He discussed questionable billing charges from water districts.

  Commissioner Anneet stated she observed resources responding to a fire in
  Northern California that were supported by homeowners who ensured defensibility
  of their property. She stated it was important to continue to educate the community
  about defensibility.

  Commissioner Spiegel discussed a slide at Puerco Canyon that shut down the
  highway for a few hours. He stated residents were forced to use canyon roads,

  Vice Chair Stewart congratulated Chair Frost for receiving the first public safety

  with Interim City Manager McClary, Public Safety Manager Dueñas, and Public
  Works Director DuBoux to discuss the Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) in

  In response to Vice Chair Stewart, Public Safety Manager Dueñas provided an
  update the status of crime mapping and installation of cameras.

  Chair Frost stated the property owner at Las Tunas contracted a weekly patrol for
  his property. He asked what would happen if flooding from a private road spread
  onto public streets. Public Works Superintendent Aladjadjian stated City staff
  would contact the property owner to mitigate the problem.

  Chair Frost asked why traffic signals in eastern Malibu went out during the storms.
  Public Works Superintendent Aladjadjian stated the City contacted Caltrans and
  was advised that signals had to be reset due to power surges that disabled the
  batteries. In response to Chair Frost, Public Works Superintendent Aladjadjian
  stated the City had nearly completed repairing and replacing signs damaged during
  the storms. He stated the City would inform Caltrans of missing or damaged signs
  on PCH. Chair Frost agreed with Ex Officio Member Woodworth about the need
  to monitor properties for fire prevention. In response to Commissioner Spiegel,
  Chair Frost discussed past events when canyon roads and the highway were closed.
  He commended Public Safety Manager Dueñas and public agencies for helping
  with the Leo Carrillo evacuation.

  Fire Safety Liaison Brossard explained the circumstances that led to the evacuation.
  In response to Commissioner Spiegel, he stated the closure of PCH at Puerco
  Canyon was necessary to allow safe clearance of mud and debris from the highway.
  He stated City staff participated in several conference calls with NOAA and the
  National Weather Service throughout the storm event.

  Public Safety Manager Dueñas stated the Public Safety team conducted strategic
  planning for 2022. She stated many of the Commissioners’ suggestions today were
  included in those discussions. She stated the plan would be presented to the
  Commission at the February meeting.

ITEM 3  OLD BUSINESS

  A.  Second Review of Parking Citation Fine Schedule

  Recommended Action: 1) Receive a report on parking citation fine implementation
  challenges; and 2) Re-evaluate previously recommended parking citation fine
  increases and revise the recommendations, if appropriate.

  Public Safety Manager Dueñas presented the report. She introduced Renée
  Neermann, Finance Manager.

  Finance Manager Neermann stated raising fines was often not a deterrent since
  people did not know the fine until they received a citation. She discussed common
  reasoning used by people to contest citations, such as confusing signage and
  markings and uncommonly shaped fire hydrants. She stated the vehicle code
  required that fines be similar to those in surrounding jurisdictions. She discussed
  phone calls accusing the City of using citations to raise revenue. She stated the City
  was obligated to provide the option of a payment plan, which required additional
  monitoring by staff or the contractor, which negated the fine.

  Commissioner Spiegel stated he disagreed with this item being brought back to the
  Commission. He stated it was important that Commission recommendations be
  taken straight to the City Council, and staff could comment directly to the Council.
  He stated Malibu was different than Las Virgenes. He stated deterrence was not the
  only consideration. He stated there needed to be punitive measures. He suggested
  presenting the Commission’s original recommendation to the City Council.

  Commissioner Anneet stated surrounding neighborhood fine structures were taken
  into account when this item was originally discussed. She stated most violations
  were obvious. Finance Manager Neermann stated remarks about confusing signage
  were shared with the Public Work Department.

  Public Safety Manager Dueñas stated the staff report attachment displayed fines
  charged by other jurisdictions. In response to Commissioner Anneet, Public Safety
  Manager Dueñas stated Santa Monica’s fines were lower on many of the citations.

  Chair Frost agreed that some signs and markings were unclear. He stated fire
  hydrants were not always clearly marked. He stated fire hydrants and their markings
  were the responsibility of Los Angeles County Waterworks District 29.

  Vice Chair Stewart stated other cities’ fine schedules were considered. He stated he
  was unaware of the Las Virgenes Parking Authority (LVPA). Finance Manager
  Neermann stated she would get additional information for the Commission.

  Public Safety Specialist Kaplan stated the LVPA included Agoura Hills, Hidden
  Hills, Westlake Village, and Calabasas.

  Vice Chair Stewart thanked Finance Manager Neermann and the hearing officer for
  their work. He stated none of the LVPA cities were beach cities with millions of
  visitors each year. He discussed the step structure for many County fines. He stated
  Santa Monica had low fines for parking but was extremely aggressive with
  violations related to bike lanes. He stated blocking streets in a high fire risk city
  like Malibu was a greater offense requiring a higher fine. He stated parking citations
  were intended to be penalties, not deterrents.

  In response to Commissioner Spiegel, Public Safety Manager Dueñas stated the
  item was brought back out of respect for the Commission and due to the new
  information found about the court case referenced in the report attachment.

  Chair Frost stated he compared many fines to those imposed by other beach cities,
  including Newport Beach and Manhattan Beach. He stated most complaints were
  about signage or the validity of a fine.

  Finance Manager Neermann stated the City received pushback about how high the
  fines were. She displayed photos of fire hydrants from parking citation appeals.

  Commissioner Anneet stated the $150.00 fines were significantly higher than any
  other fine in the City. She agreed with Chair Frost that Malibu was more
  comparable to Manhattan Beach and Newport Beach.

  Ex Officio Member Woodworth stated there were six categories where the
  recommended increased fine was much higher than the comparable fine schedules.

  Chair Frost displayed a photo of a disconnected trailer parked in the PCH median.
  He discussed visitors parking trailers then driving their vehicle out of town. In
  response to Chair Frost, Finance Manager Neermann explained the process staff
  used with callers challenging a citation.

  In response to Chair Frost, Mark Russo, Volunteers on Patrol (VOP), stated the
  VOP issued 17,092 parking citations in 2021 for a total of $1.145 million in fines.
  Finance Manager Neermann clarified that not all fines were collected since some
  fines were reduced or appealed. Mr. Russo explained the VOP’s role in the process,
  including educating the public. He stated most people knew they were in violation
  of parking regulations. He stated consistency was important. He stated VOPs
  communicated with City staff about parking issues.

  Fire Safety Liaison Brossard agreed many hydrants were confusing, especially
  those set off from the roadway. He suggested a red line should be painted on the
  ground by the hydrant. He suggested signage indicating the fire hydrant and
  distance of no parking should be considered. He stated Malibu’s fire hydrant system
  was inconsistent.

  Public Safety Manager Dueñas stated ways to improve markings for hydrants could
  be discussed at a future meeting.

MOTION  Vice Chair Stewart moved and Chair Frost seconded a motion to affirm the
  previously recommended parking citation fine increases for presentation to the City
  Council. The question was called, and the motion carried 4-0, Commissioner Gibbs
  absent.

ITEM 4  NEW BUSINESS

  A.  Public Safety Agency Activity
  Recommended Action: Discuss recent Public Safety Agency activities and receive
  and file activity reports from the County of Los Angeles Sheriff’s Department, Fire
  Department, and Lifeguard Division.

  Vice Chair Stewart discussed the increase in fatal accidents on PCH. He suggested
  the barrier that resulted in a recent bicyclist fatality be investigated.

ADJOURNMENT

MOTION  At 6:35 p.m., Chair Frost moved and Commissioner Spiegel seconded a motion to
  adjourn. The question was called, and the motion carried 4-0, Commissioner Gibbs
  absent.

  5.A.
  Public Safety Commission
  Agenda Report
To:  Chair Frost and Members of the Public Safety Commission

Prepared by:  Susan Dueñas, Public Safety Manager

Approved by:  Steve McClary, Interim City Manager

Date prepared:  January 20, 2022  Meeting date:  February 2, 2022

Subject:  Public Safety Goals for 2022

RECOMMENDED ACTION: Receive and file a report regarding goals for the City’s Public
Safety Office in 2022 and provide feedback to staff.

DISCUSSION:  On January 4, 2022, Public Safety staff reviewed their current projects
and outstanding needs, identifying five overarching goals for 2022 along with supporting
actions to achieve the goals. The supporting actions are also in line with time constraints
and available funding.

The overarching goals include:
  • Reduce the risk and impact of a wildfire
  • Reduce the number of people living unhoused in Malibu by 30%
  • Increase preparedness for a damaging earthquake
  • Increase public safety presence in the community
  • Improve safety on Pacific Coast Highway

Many of the supporting actions (Attached) are not new initiatives; however, the following
are new:

Home Hardening Support
The City’s Fire Safety Liaisons will continue the home ignition zone assessment program
but will seek to secure grant funding to help offset the cost and incentivize homeowners
to implement the recommended home hardening projects. In addition, they will reach out
to homeowner associations to identify hazard reduction projects for their neighborhoods.

  Page 1 of 3
  Agenda Item # 5.A.
 Brush Clearance Enforcement
The Los Angeles County Fire Department (LACFD) performs annual brush clearance
inspections prior to its June 1st deadline. Property owners who are found to be out of
compliance are sent letters advising them of the hazards that need to be mitigated.
Property owners are then given additional time to bring the property into compliance before
being reinspected. If property owners do not comply after multiple opportunities, the case
is transferred to the LACoFD Brush Clearance Unit (for improved properties) or the Los
Angeles County Agricultural Commissioner/Weights and Measures (ACWM) (for
unimproved properties). These two units may perform the work necessary and assess
the cost for the work on the property’s annual property tax statement. However, City
staff regularly receives complaints from neighbors that enforcement is not being done.
While most property owners comply, it has been observed that enforcement follow-through
on out of compliance properties is insufficient and some property owners who are out of
compliance are not identified during the regular inspections. Staff intends to work with
LACoFD and ACWM to review how the inspections and enforcement are being done and
look for ways the City can support brush clearance inspections and enforcement follow-
through.

Earthquake Preparedness
Public Safety staff recognize that wildfire is the community’s most frequent threat and has
the greatest potential to destroy homes. However, the City is also vulnerable to a
catastrophic earthquake that could lead to loss of life, structural damage and widespread
infrastructure disruption. Fortunately, many wildfire preparedness actions also support
earthquake preparedness, but there are some key differences that need to be addressed.
For example, the City’s most vulnerable buildings are soft-story structures. The term “soft-
story” refers to one level of a building that is significantly more flexible or weak in lateral
load resistance than the stories above it and the floors or the foundation below it, such as
tuck-under parking beneath wood-framed residential apartment buildings. In the 1994
Northridge Earthquake, the catastrophic collapse of the Northridge Meadows apartments
was due to this type of construction. Many other cities have established requirements for
soft-story structures to be retrofitted, such as the cities of Los Angeles, Santa Monica, and
West Hollywood, which all adopted ordinances that require soft-story structures be fully
retrofitted by 2023. It is not being suggested at this time that a similar ordinance be put
into place in Malibu; however, assessing how many buildings need to be retrofitted, as
well as exploring strategies to encourage property owners to retrofit their buildings, needs
to be done. Also, a large-scale, regional earthquake will likely impact local infrastructure
in ways not experienced in the past. The first step to understanding and addressing that
potential threat is to conduct a comprehensive threat assessment with the City’s first
responder and critical infrastructure partners. Staff recommends that this be coordinated
through the City’s Disaster Council. The goals of the assessment would be to identify
capability gaps and develop strategies for closing and/or mitigating the gaps.

  Page 2 of 3
  Agenda Item # 5.A.
 Public Safety Presence
The supporting actions to increase public safety presence in the community are meant to
create more opportunities for interaction between staff and community members. The
City’s two Fire Safety Liaisons spend a lot of time in the community, which increases their
awareness of community issues and familiarity with different neighborhoods, as well as
providing visibility and an opportunity to proactively identify and address safety concerns.
Building on this model, all Public Safety staff will now conduct regular field checks in
vehicles marked as Malibu Public Safety. Staff will also actively seek out opportunities to
attend neighborhood and community meetings, as well as offer customized presentations
to groups. Lastly, staff will explore the potential to have Sheriff’s vehicles marked as
serving “Malibu.”

PCH Safety
Pacific Coast Highway (PCH) has long been a major safety concern for the community,
and the last year was particularly hazardous with nine fatalities. Efforts by the Los Angeles
County Sheriff’s Department, Caltrans, the City’s Public Works Department, and the PCH
Task Force have all made a difference, but there is always more to be done. Public Safety
staff recognize that maintenance and law enforcement on PCH is handled by other
agencies, but due to the significant safety concerns, staff will make an extra effort to assist
by looking more critically at PCH while traveling in town. Any safety issues that are
observed will be noted, and Public Safety staff will follow up with the appropriate agency
to determine if it is already being addressed or needs to be addressed.

The 2022 goals and supporting actions are meant to provide a clear plan for making
significant public safety improvements in the community while remaining flexible to
address other needs and priorities as they arise. Staff recommends that the Commission
review the Public Safety Goals for 2022 and provide feedback as appropriate.

ATTACHMENTS: Public Safety Goals for 2022

  Page 3 of 3
  Agenda Item # 5.A.
   Public Safety Goals for 2022
REDUCE THE RISK AND IMPACT OF A WILDFIRE
  - Complete Beacon Box program implementation
  - Work with neighborhoods/HOA on hazard reduction projects for their neighborhoods
  - Continue working with Fire Brigade program
  - Develop a video to encourage and illustrate the value of evacuation
  - Work with Los Angeles County Fire Department to improve brush clearance enforcement
  - Monitor, identify and clear encampments in the brush
  - Host Home Ignition Zone Assessment Training for the community
  - Conduct four fire extinguisher training classes
  - Develop incentives and encourage residents to implement home hardening strategies

INCREASE PREPAREDNESS FOR A DAMAGING EARTHQUAKE
  - Conduct an earthquake threat assessment in coordination with the Malibu Disaster Council
  - Provide leadership training for Malibu CERT Team
  - Reach out to community organizations to assess strengths and needs during disasters
  - Identify capabilities of all telecommunication providers and status of back-up power
  - Conduct at least two CERT classes (COVID permitting)
  - Provide earthquake-specific training for CERT Team
  - Update equipment and resources in the City’s Emergency Operations Center (EOC)
  - Fully stock the Zuma and Las Flores emergency bins
  - Identify soft-story structures and develop incentives for retrofitting
  - Continue to support communications improvements, such as FM Alert

INCREASE PUBLIC SAFETY PRESENCE IN THE COMMUNITY
  - Place Malibu Public Safety car magnets on City fleet cars and conduct regular field checks
  - Work with Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department to add Malibu decal to patrol cars
  - Develop a Public Safety Resource Guide
  - Host annual Public Safety Expo with emphasis on fire and earthquake
  - Conduct direct outreach to neighborhoods, homeowner associations and other community groups

REDUCE THE NUMBER OF PEOPLE LIVING UNHOUSED IN MALIBU BY 30%
  - Support the Outreach Team in connecting individuals to services and housing
  - Support the Homelessness Task Force and Homelessness Working Group
  - Implement strategies approved by the City Council
  - Monitor and identify encampments on private property
  - Support trespassing enforcement by maintaining an up-to-date Letter of Agency file
  - Work with the Sheriff’s Department to enforce the camping ordinance
  - Work with the Sheriff’s Department to enforce the Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zone (VHFHSZ)
  ordinance

IMPROVE SAFETY ON PCH
  - Take note of hazards observed on PCH
  - Work with appropriate agencies to mitigate identified hazards

  NOTEWORTHY INCIDENTS

  A resident was arrested for assault in the area of Pacific Coast Highway and
  Westward Beach Road. The suspect assaulted the victim with a metal baseball
  bat. The victim and suspect were roommates and were having ongoing disputes.
  (21-07519)

  Four incidents of assault were reported this month that were committed by the
  same suspect in the area of Pacific Coast Highway and Tuna Canyon Road.
  All four victims and the suspect are currently unhoused and transient in nature.
  The suspect attacked the victims while they were sleeping in the area. Three
  of the victims suffered lacerations from an edged weapon for non-life-threatening
  injuries. The fourth victim was able to defend himself and the suspect fled the
  area. The investigations are ongoing. (21-07094, 07097, 07162, 07163)

  A transient was arrested for residential burglary in the 20800 block of Pacific
  Coast Highway. A spare house key under a pot in the front yard was used
  by the suspect to make entry into the residence. The stolen property was
  recovered during the arrest. (21-07129)

  A resident of Santa Monica was arrested for burglary and arson in the 30100
  block of Morning View Drive. The suspect used a tree stump to smash the front
  window next to the front door of the location (a church). Ten bibles were set on
  fire on top of a table inside the location. Another fire was also started in the
  driveway of a residence in the 30100 block of Morning View Drive. (21-07192)

  A Lynwood resident was arrested for theft from a vehicle that occurred in the
  area of Pacific Coast Highway and Webb Way in November 2021. Property
  stolen consisted of vehicle registration paperwork and a vehicle battery.
  (21-06776)

  FEBRUARY 2,2022
  TELECONFERENCED VARIOUS LOCATIONS

  5:00 P.M.

The following meeting was held pursuant to AB 361 and fully teleconferenced from various
locations during the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic.

CALL TO ORDER

  Chair Frost called the meeting to order at 5:00 p.m.

ROLL CALL

  The following persons were recorded in attendance by the Recording Secretary:

  PRESENT: Chair Chris Frost; Vice Chair Doug Stewart; Commissioners Daphne Anneet
  (arrived at 5:07 p.m.), Keegan Gibbs, and Joshua Spiegel; and Ex Officio Member Brent
